newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: PRIME MINISTER SAYS FARMERS HAVE NOTHING TO FEAR
Prime Minister John Howard has assured farmers he respects the contribution they make to Australia's export earnings and is not about to let them down on Native Title.
John Howard was addressing about 500 Liberal Party faithful at a lunch in Brisbane today
Mr Howard says he'll go on trying to find a solution to the Wik decision that satisfies all parties, but pastoralists have nothing to fear.
CABINET DEFERS RADIO AUSTRALIA DECISION

Federal Cabinet has deferred making a decision about the future of the ABC's overseas broadcast service, Radio Australia. Cabinet today discussed a submission from the ABC that calls for the closure or substantial reduction of Radio Australia as one of its budget cutting options.
One proposal under consideration was a plan to reduce Radio Australia to an English-language satellite service.
The ABC submission says the total closure of the international service would save 20-million dollars a year.
A spokesman for Communications Minister Richard Alston says although Radio Australia's future was addressed at today's meeting, no final decision was made.
TELSTRA NOT COMMENTING ON SPECIAL DIVIDEND CLAIMS
Telstra is refusing to comment on reports it's being asked to pay a three billion dollar special dividend to the Federal Government, to help reduce the budget deficit.
Telstra reportedly is preparing to borrow the money and is looking for prospective underwriters.
The Federal Opposition is describing the move as a massive budget fiddle and claims telephone users will have the pay the hundreds of millions of dollars in interest payments on this loan every year.
A spokesman for Telstra would not be drawn on the story, while Communication Minister Richard Alston's office says any such loan would be a matter for Telstra's board.
AIRSHIP TRIAL OVER SYDNEY FOR 12 MONTHS
Sydney's concerns about aircraft noise have been put aside in a decision to give an airship permission to fly over the city for a 12 month trial.
The Administrative Appeals Tribunal today overturned the Federal Transport Department's earlier decision not to give approval to the airship.
The Department believed the airship would have had an adverse effect on the Sydney community, which it claimed is far more sensitive to aircraft noise than elsewhere.
The Tribunal has imposed eight conditions on the airship, including it be restricted to flights between six o'clock in the morning and ten p-m.
OPPOSITION SAYS GOVT NEEDS TO RETHINK BUDGET STRATEGY
The Federal Opposition says it's time for the Government to rethink its budget strategy, after the release of job-related figures today.
Shadow Employment Minister Martin Ferguson says figures from the Bureau of Statistics show unemployment in 77-per cent of regional areas has risen sharply or stagnated since the Coalition won office.
Mr Ferguson says unemployment outside the Sydney and Melbourne metropolitan areas has risen to more than 10 per cent, and in regional Queensland the jobless rate is now 11-point-five per cent.
He says the Government's economic policies are clearly hurting regional Australia, with 77-per cent of rural and regional Australians now worse off.
NFF SAYS POLLS SHOW WIK ADS NOT RACIST
The National Farmers' Federation says independent polling about its recent television advertising campaign on Wik shows most people believed the ads were not racist.
Aboriginal leaders suspended roundtable negotiations with the NFF on pastoral leases and native title because of the ads, which they said were racist.
The NFF says the poll of city dwellers it commissioned shows 82-per cent believed the ads were not racist, and 58 per cent believed the plight of farmers was genuine or believable.
The NFF says a lot of people in city homes and boardrooms now understand the High Court's Wik decision poses the biggest threat, ever, to the rural sector.
COWLEY TO STEP DOWN FROM NEWS LTD
The Executive Chairman of News Limited, Ken Cowley, has announced he's retiring at the end of June.
Mr Cowley has been with News Limited for 33 years, joining Rupert Murdoch in 1964 to launch "The Australian" newspaper.
Overall responsibility of News Limited's Australian operations will be assumed by Lachlan Murdoch.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
